name: Korean exfoliating mitt
lead: The Korean exfoliating mitt, also sold as an Italy towel or kessa-style mitt, is a coarse viscose or nylon glove used to scrub the body, typically after soaking in warm water or a bath. The scrubbing produces visible rolls of loosened dead skin and is associated with Korean bathhouse bathing culture.

In appearance care it is used for smoother, more even-looking body skin and a short-term glow. The site rates the effect as temporary. It is a form of physical (mechanical) exfoliation, which is the removal of dead cells from the outermost skin layer, the stratum corneum [1]. Published research specific to the mitt is very limited; the one directly relevant paper found examined biophysical changes after mechanical injury to the stratum corneum [2].

paras: The mitt is a fitted glove with a rough textile surface. It is generally used on wet, warm skin, and the friction rolls off the outer layer of skin as small grey strands that users find visually satisfying. Grokipedia, an AI-generated encyclopedia, defines exfoliation in cosmetology as removal of dead skin cells from the stratum corneum to promote renewal and improve texture, and lists physical tools and scrubs alongside chemical and enzymatic methods [1].

Warm water softens and swells the stratum corneum, and friction then sheds the outer layers. Skin cell turnover is continuous: cells produced in the basal layer move outward, flatten and become the anucleated corneocytes of the stratum corneum, which sit in a lipid matrix that provides barrier function [1]. According to the same source, over-exfoliation, especially with aggressive physical methods, can disrupt the barrier and cause irritation, and typical advice is to tailor frequency to skin type [1].
No clinical trials of Korean exfoliating mitts as a product were found.

A 2002 paper titled Biophysical changes after mechanical injury of the stratum corneum in normal skin examined how the skin barrier and related properties respond to mechanical disruption of the stratum corneum [2]. The site's research notes describe it as a small study in which a single scrubbing session temporarily reduced water-holding capacity, which recovered within a few days, while repeated scrubbing shortened stratum corneum turnover time without a measurable change in barrier function. These details have not been reproduced here from the abstract and should be read as secondary.

Grokipedia reports that aggressive physical exfoliation can cause barrier disruption, irritation, and worsening of acne or sensitivity [1]. Dermatological sources more generally describe redness, micro-tears and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation as possible consequences of over-scrubbing, particularly on darker skin and on inflamed skin. Moisturiser use afterwards is commonly advised. The grey rolls produced are described in the site's notes as dead skin and soap residue rather than toxins.

The mitt is listed in the body-care category as an inexpensive full-body exfoliant. Forum threads retrieved for this entry did not discuss it in substance, so no community protocol or claims could be documented.

refs.title: Biophysical changes after mechanical injury of the stratum corneum in normal skin
